EL PASO, Texas (CNN) -- The cell phone rang as Jorge Aguirre walked to a friend's funeral in Juarez, Mexico, last November -- a funeral for a fellow journalist who, Aguirre says, was assassinated for the critical stories he wrote. Mexican federal police recently began patrolling Ciudad Juarez, just across the border from El Paso, Texas. When he answered the phone, Aguirre heard a profanity-laced threat. "They told me I was next," Aguirre told CNN. "I thought they were going to kill me right there." Aguirre immediately gathered up his family and darted across the border into El Paso, Texas. He hasn't returned to Juarez since that day. Aguirre is seeking asylum in the United States, and he's part of a growing trend among Mexican citizens looking to escape the violence and corruption of their homeland.  Watch journalists met with death threats » . According to the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, an agency that falls under the Department of Homeland Security, the number of Mexican nationals requesting asylum in the United States based on "credible fear" has gone up every year since 2003, even as the overall number of "credible fear" asylum cases remains steady. In 2003, the USCIS reported 54 asylum cases from Mexican citizens. In 2008, that number reached 312. But asylum requests based on fear of violence aren't easy cases to make. Last year, the United States approved less than half of those cases. "Whether they're fleeing extortionists or potential kidnappers or they're leaving because of the drug cartels, it tells you there are definitely problems in Mexico right now," said El Paso Mayor John Cook. Those seeking asylum come from every walk of life. There are journalists, entrepreneurs and even law enforcement officials, including three police chiefs. For Raymond Cobos, the sheriff in Luna County, New Mexico, this is the most disturbing revelation. Just across the Mexican border is a dusty, far-flung outpost called Palomas, a speck of a town that's a popular path for drug trafficking and human smuggling. It's also been the site of wild gunbattles between cops and the cartels. The cartels outgunned the police force, and the police chief disappeared and sought asylum in the United States. It's not clear where his case stands or where the police chief is today. "I don't know what I would do. It's pretty hard to fight that type of situation by yourself -- if you're in an environment that you don't know from one day to the next if someone's going to knock on your door and blast your family away," Cobos said. Emilio Gutierrez is another journalist hiding in El Paso. He wrote stories critical of the Mexican government for a small newspaper in the northern Mexico state of Chihuahua, which shares a border with Texas and New Mexico.  Watch cops say U.S. teens were cartel hit men » . Last May, Gutierrez says men dressed in Mexican military fatigues raided his home in the middle of the night. He was told they were looking for drugs and weapons. A month later, a friend called, frantically urging him to hide. Gutierrez grabbed his family, drove to El Paso and requested asylum. He spent seven months in a U.S. jail as his case moved through the immigration system. He's recently been allowed to leave the jail while his request is pending. He's now in hiding in El Paso. "The fear never ends," Gutierrez told CNN. "We're scared for our families that are still on the other side, and we're scared for ourselves." Gutierrez and Aguirre offer a chilling perspective on everyday life in areas of Mexico that are consumed with violence and corruption. They describe a situation that has left ordinary citizens unable to trust anyone in positions of authority. "Thousands of families are in danger of being killed," Aguirre said. "They're vulnerable because they can't go to the police for help because that might get them killed."

Mexican federal police had recently begun patrolling Ciudad Juarez, just across the border from El Paso, Texas. When Aguirre answered the call, he heard a profanity-laced threat.

“They told me I was next,” Aguirre told CNN. “I thought they were going to kill me right there.”

Aguirre immediately gathered his family and fled across the border into El Paso. He has not returned to Juarez since.

Now seeking asylum in the United States, Aguirre is part of a growing trend of Mexican citizens trying to escape the violence and corruption in their homeland. Watch journalists met with death threats ».

According to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, an agency within the Department of Homeland Security, the number of Mexican nationals requesting asylum in the United States based on “credible fear” has increased every year since 2003, even as the overall number of “credible fear” asylum cases has remained steady.

In 2003, USCIS reported 54 asylum cases involving Mexican citizens. By 2008, that number had risen to 312. But asylum requests based on fear of violence are difficult to prove. Last year, the United States approved fewer than half of such cases.

“Whether they’re fleeing extortionists or potential kidnappers or they’re leaving because of the drug cartels, it tells you there are definitely problems in Mexico right now,” said El Paso Mayor John Cook.

Those seeking asylum come from every walk of life. They include journalists, entrepreneurs, and even law enforcement officials, among them three police chiefs.

For Raymond Cobos, the sheriff of Luna County, New Mexico, that is the most troubling revelation.

Just across the Mexican border lies Palomas, a dusty, remote outpost—a tiny town that has become a popular route for drug trafficking and human smuggling. It has also been the scene of fierce gun battles between police and the cartels.

The cartels outgunned the police force, and the police chief disappeared and sought asylum in the United States. It is unclear where his case stands or where the police chief is today.

“I don’t know what I would do. It’s pretty hard to fight that type of situation by yourself -- if you’re in an environment that you don’t know from one day to the next if someone’s going to knock on your door and blast your family away,” Cobos said.

Emilio Gutierrez is another journalist now hiding in El Paso. He wrote stories critical of the Mexican government for a small newspaper in Chihuahua, the northern Mexican state that borders Texas and New Mexico. Watch cops say U.S. teens were cartel hit men ».

Gutierrez gathered his family, drove to El Paso, and requested asylum. He spent seven months in a U.S. jail while his case moved through the immigration system. He has recently been permitted to leave the jail while his request remains pending. He is now in hiding in El Paso.

“The fear never ends,” Gutierrez told CNN. “We’re scared for our families that are still on the other side, and we’re scared for ourselves.”

Gutierrez and Aguirre offer a chilling perspective on everyday life in areas of Mexico consumed by violence and corruption. They describe conditions that have left ordinary citizens unable to trust anyone in positions of authority.

People requesting asylum come from many different backgrounds. They include reporters, business owners and members of law enforcement, among them three police chiefs.

For Raymond Cobos, sheriff of Luna County, New Mexico, that fact is especially alarming.

“I don’t know what I would do. It’s pretty hard to fight that type of situation by yourself -- if you’re in an environment that you don’t know from one day to the next if someone’s going to knock on your door and blast your family away,” Cobos said.

Another journalist now living in hiding in El Paso is Emilio Gutierrez. He had written articles criticizing the Mexican government for a small newspaper in Chihuahua, a northern Mexican state bordering Texas and New Mexico.

Last May, Gutierrez said, men wearing Mexican military uniforms broke into his house in the middle of the night. They told him they were searching for drugs and weapons.

One month later, a friend called him in a panic and urged him to go into hiding. Gutierrez took his family, drove to El Paso and applied for asylum.

“The fear never ends,” Gutierrez told CNN. “We’re scared for our families that are still on the other side, and we’re scared for ourselves.”

counterfactuals.output:
**EL PASO, Texas —** Mexican journalists and police officials fleeing threats from drug cartels and corrupt authorities in Ciudad Juarez and the state of Chihuahua are increasingly turning to the United States for protection, saying the violence they investigated, reported on or tried to stop has followed them to their doorsteps.

At border crossings near El Paso, asylum seekers from northern Mexico have described a grim pattern: anonymous calls, surveillance outside their homes, murdered colleagues, and warnings that they would be next if they refused to cooperate or stay silent.

Some are reporters who covered cartel killings, extortion and government corruption. Others are current or former police officers who say they were targeted after refusing bribes, arresting cartel members or reporting collusion between criminals and officials.

“I could not trust the criminals, and I could not trust some of the people wearing uniforms,” one former law enforcement official from Chihuahua said in an account shared with immigration advocates. “When that happens, there is nowhere left to go.”

Their cases highlight the continuing danger in parts of northern Mexico, where organized crime groups have long battled for control of drug-trafficking routes, migrant smuggling corridors and local institutions. Ciudad Juarez, across the Rio Grande from El Paso, has for years been one of the most closely watched cities in Mexico’s struggle against cartel violence.

Press freedom organizations have repeatedly identified Mexico as one of the most dangerous countries in the world for journalists outside active war zones. Reporters who investigate organized crime or political corruption often face threats not only from cartel members but also from public officials accused of working with criminal groups.

Asylum attorneys in El Paso say Mexican applicants can face a difficult legal path in the United States. To win asylum, they must show they have been persecuted or have a well-founded fear of persecution because of a protected ground, such as political opinion or membership in a particular social group. Generalized violence, even severe violence, is often not enough.

That burden can be especially challenging for police officers and journalists, whose claims may depend on proving they were targeted not merely because of their work, but because of what their work represented — opposition to corruption, refusal to collaborate with cartels or exposure of official misconduct.

Immigration advocates say many applicants arrive with police reports, news clippings, threatening messages or documentation of attacks against colleagues. But they also say some victims never reported threats in Mexico because they believed local authorities were compromised.

For journalists, the decision to flee often means abandoning not only a home but a profession. Some say they can no longer publish under their own names. Others have stopped reporting altogether, fearing their families could be harmed if they continue.

Police officials who seek asylum face a different stigma. Some worry they will be viewed with suspicion because of the widespread infiltration of law enforcement by organized crime. But advocates say those who resist corruption can be among the most vulnerable.

“They are caught between the cartel that wants obedience and the corrupt official who wants silence,” one El Paso-based immigration attorney said. “If they refuse both, they become targets.”

The violence in Chihuahua has also had ripple effects in El Paso, where families, churches and legal aid groups have helped asylum seekers navigate the immigration system. Many applicants wait months or years for their cases to be decided, often unable to return to Mexico and uncertain whether they will be allowed to remain in the United States permanently.

U.S. immigration officials do not publicly discuss individual asylum cases. The Department of Homeland Security has said asylum claims are reviewed under U.S. law and that applicants must establish eligibility based on the facts of their cases.

For those who fled Ciudad Juarez and Chihuahua, the legal arguments are complex, but their fear is immediate.

“They knew where I lived,” said one journalist who left northern Mexico after receiving threats tied to coverage of organized crime. “They knew my family. After that, every car outside the house looked like danger.”

Across the border in El Paso, the skyline of Juarez is visible just a short distance away. For many seeking asylum, that closeness is both a comfort and a reminder: home is near, but returning could be deadly.

counterfactuals.output:
**Mexican Journalists’ Flight Highlights Rise in U.S. “Credible Fear” Claims**

*By [Reporter Name]*

**EL PASO, Texas —** When Mexican journalist **Jorge Luis Aguirre** crossed into the United States after receiving death threats in Ciudad Juárez, he joined a growing stream of Mexicans telling U.S. immigration officers they feared returning home. Another reporter, **Emilio Gutiérrez Soto**, had made a similar journey after alleging threats from Mexican military personnel following his reporting on abuses in Chihuahua.

Their cases have become emblematic of a broader trend: a rise in Mexican asylum seekers who pass through the U.S. “credible fear” screening system, a first step for many migrants who arrive at or between ports of entry and say they face persecution or torture if deported.

According to **U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS)** Asylum Division data, credible-fear referrals have increased sharply over the past two decades as more migrants from Mexico and other countries have sought protection at the border. USCIS has reported that overall credible-fear receipts rose from **fewer than 10,000 annually in the mid-2000s** to **more than 90,000 in fiscal year 2018**, over **100,000 in fiscal year 2019**, and later surged again amid post-pandemic migration increases, reaching **well over 100,000 cases annually** in recent years.

Mexicans have represented a significant share of these claims, especially during periods of intense cartel violence and attacks on civil society. USCIS statistics from the late 2000s and early 2010s showed a notable increase in Mexican credible-fear claims as violence escalated in states such as Chihuahua, Tamaulipas, Michoacán and Guerrero. While not every credible-fear finding results in asylum, a positive screening allows migrants to pursue protection before an immigration judge or asylum officer.

### Journalists under threat

Aguirre, a journalist and founder of the border news site **LaPolaka.com**, fled Ciudad Juárez in 2008 after a wave of murders, intimidation and corruption linked to organized crime. His departure came amid the killing of journalists and media workers in one of Mexico’s most dangerous cities.

He has said he received threats after reporting on organized crime and official corruption. His asylum case drew attention from press-freedom organizations, which argued that Mexican journalists faced not only cartel violence but also weak protection from authorities and impunity for attackers.

Gutiérrez Soto, a former reporter for **El Diario del Noroeste** in Chihuahua, fled Mexico with his son after reporting on alleged abuses by members of the Mexican military. He sought asylum in the United States, arguing that returning to Mexico would place him in grave danger.

His case became one of the most closely watched Mexican journalist asylum cases in the U.S. It also underscored how difficult such claims can be: applicants must show they were targeted on account of a protected ground — such as political opinion or membership in a particular social group — and that their government is unable or unwilling to protect them.

### Credible fear is only the first hurdle

Under U.S. law, “credible fear” is a preliminary screening for people subject to expedited removal who say they fear persecution or torture. The standard is lower than the standard for winning asylum. If USCIS asylum officers find a “significant possibility” that the person could qualify for protection, the case may proceed.

But passing the credible-fear interview does not guarantee asylum. Many applicants wait years in immigration court backlogs, and Mexican asylum seekers historically have faced relatively low grant rates compared with applicants from some countries experiencing civil war or nationwide political repression.

Immigration lawyers say Mexican claims can be difficult because applicants must distinguish generalized criminal violence from persecution tied to a protected legal category. Journalists, human-rights defenders, political activists and people targeted for resisting cartels may have stronger claims, but success depends heavily on documentation and the facts of each case.

### Violence and impunity in Mexico

Press-freedom groups have repeatedly ranked Mexico among the most dangerous countries in the world for journalists outside active war zones. Reporters covering organized crime, corruption, policing and local politics are especially vulnerable.

Advocacy organizations have documented killings, disappearances, threats and forced displacement of journalists across Mexico. Many attacks go unsolved, contributing to a climate in which reporters censor themselves, flee their communities or leave the country.

For asylum seekers such as Aguirre and Gutiérrez, the question before U.S. authorities has been whether threats from criminal groups, soldiers or local power networks amount to persecution — and whether the Mexican state can provide meaningful protection.

### A border-region phenomenon

The rise in Mexican credible-fear claims has been especially visible along the southwest border, where asylum seekers often present themselves at ports of entry or are placed in expedited-removal proceedings after crossing without authorization.

USCIS data show that credible-fear screenings have become a major part of the asylum system’s workload. In some recent years, the agency completed tens of thousands of interviews, with historically high approval rates at the screening stage. However, final asylum outcomes are much lower after full adjudication.

That gap has fueled political debate. Supporters of asylum access say the credible-fear process is essential for preventing deportations to danger. Critics argue that the system is overburdened and that many claims ultimately fail.

For threatened journalists, advocates say the stakes are clear.

“Mexican reporters who expose organized crime and corruption can be targeted from multiple directions,” press-freedom advocates have argued in similar cases. “When local authorities cannot or will not protect them, asylum may be their only route to safety.”

### Cases that shaped attention

Aguirre’s and Gutiérrez’s cases helped draw U.S. attention to Mexican journalists as a category of asylum seekers facing unique risks. Their stories also complicated common perceptions of Mexican migration as primarily economic.

Both men fled not because of joblessness, but because of threats tied to their work.

As credible-fear claims continue to rise across nationalities, Mexican applicants remain part of a larger question confronting the U.S. asylum system: how to evaluate people fleeing a blend of cartel power, state weakness, corruption and targeted violence.

For journalists who have crossed the border with notebooks, hard drives and death threats, the answer can determine whether they rebuild their lives in safety — or are sent back to the danger they reported on.

**Mexican Families Flee Cartel Violence, Seek Safety Across Border in Texas**

*EL PASO, Texas —* A growing number of Mexican citizens say they are fleeing cartel intimidation, kidnappings and extortion in their home communities and crossing into West Texas in search of protection, adding new pressure to border shelters, local officials and law enforcement agencies across the region.

In El Paso, nonprofit shelters and city-supported intake operations have reported seeing families and individuals from northern Mexican states who say they no longer feel safe returning home.

“We didn’t leave because we wanted to,” said one asylum seeker from Chihuahua, who asked to be identified only as *María* out of fear for relatives still in Mexico. “They came to our business and told us we had to pay. When we couldn’t, they threatened my husband. We packed what we could and left that night.”

Another man, *Jorge*, said his family crossed after armed men began demanding money from residents in his town. “You don’t call the police because you don’t know who is working with who,” he said. “We came here because we needed somewhere our children could sleep.”

El Paso officials say the city has had to balance humanitarian concerns with limited local resources. A city spokesperson said local agencies are coordinating with federal immigration authorities and nonprofit partners to help process migrants and connect them with temporary shelter.

“Our priority is to ensure that people are treated safely and humanely while also protecting the stability of city services,” the official said. “El Paso has experience responding to changing migration patterns, but the demand can shift quickly.”

The situation has also drawn attention from law enforcement in neighboring New Mexico, where authorities say cartel-related violence south of the border can have ripple effects in rural communities and along transportation corridors.

A New Mexico law enforcement official said agencies remain alert for human smuggling, drug trafficking and potential spillover violence, though they emphasized that asylum seekers themselves are often victims.

“We’re watching the border region closely,” the official said. “The people arriving to request protection are frequently fleeing the same criminal organizations we investigate in other contexts. Our job is to separate public-safety threats from families who are simply trying to survive.”

Immigration attorneys say Mexican asylum claims can be difficult to win, even when applicants describe serious threats, because U.S. law requires people to show they face persecution on specific protected grounds and that their government is unwilling or unable to protect them.

Still, advocates argue the fear driving many families north is real.

“These are people caught between cartel control and limited protection at home,” said a border-area legal advocate. “For many of them, leaving is not an economic decision. It is an emergency decision.”

Federal officials have not announced a special policy for Mexican nationals fleeing cartel violence, and many migrants must wait for court dates that can be months or years away. In the meantime, families who cross into Texas often move on to sponsors elsewhere in the United States, while others remain in the El Paso area.

For María, the next step is uncertain. She says she hopes to apply for asylum and eventually work legally, but her immediate concern is safety.

“I know nothing is guaranteed,” she said. “But here, at least for now, my children are not hearing gunshots.”

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a detailed CNN article datelined El Paso, Texas, about Mexican journalists receiving death threats, crossing into the U.S., and applying for asylum amid worsening violence in northern Mexico.
counterfactuals.output:
**El Paso, Texas (CNN) —** By the time the first threat arrived, the journalist had already learned to read the signs.

A pickup circling the block outside his home. A stranger asking neighbors about his routine. A message delivered through a contact who told him, quietly, that his reporting had angered the wrong people.

Then came the call.

“Stop publishing,” the voice said, according to the reporter, who asked to be identified only by a pseudonym, “Luis,” because he fears reprisals against relatives still in Mexico. “You know what happens to people who don’t listen.”

Within days, Luis packed a small bag, gathered copies of his articles and police complaints, and headed north from Mexico’s border region toward El Paso, Texas. At a port of entry, he told US officials he was afraid to return home and wanted to request asylum.

He is now one of a growing number of Mexican journalists who say they have been forced to flee as violence and intimidation intensify across parts of northern Mexico — a region where organized crime, political corruption and local power struggles have made reporting increasingly dangerous.

Press freedom advocates say journalists in Mexican border states face a uniquely perilous mix: criminal groups seeking to control public information, local officials angered by investigations into corruption, and weak institutions that often fail to investigate attacks. For some reporters, crossing into the United States has become the last remaining option.

“We don’t leave because we want a better job,” Luis said from a temporary shelter in El Paso. “We leave because staying alive becomes the only story that matters.”

## Threats after reporting on crime and corruption

Luis spent more than a decade covering crime, disappearances and municipal politics in northern Mexico. His work often focused on alleged links between local officials and criminal organizations — the kind of reporting that journalists in the region say can quickly draw attention from both sides.

The threats escalated after he published a story about a suspected criminal network operating with apparent impunity, he said. Soon after, he began receiving messages warning him to stop naming certain people. One message included details about his child’s school schedule.

“That was when I understood they were not just angry,” he said. “They were watching.”

CNN could not independently verify all the threats described by Luis, but he provided copies of messages, news clippings and a complaint he says he filed with Mexican authorities. Like several journalists interviewed in El Paso and Ciudad Juárez, he said official protection mechanisms were either slow, insufficient or inaccessible in the moment he needed them most.

Mexico has a federal protection mechanism for journalists and human rights defenders, designed to provide emergency measures such as panic buttons, police patrols and relocation support. But press advocates have long criticized it as underfunded and unable to address the deeper problem: impunity.

“Protection cannot simply be a phone number you call after the threat,” said a press freedom advocate familiar with cases along the border. “If attacks are not investigated and perpetrators are not punished, the message is that silencing a journalist works.”

## A dangerous country for journalists

Mexico has for years ranked among the most dangerous countries in the world for journalists outside active war zones, according to international press freedom organizations. Reporters covering organized crime, local politics, police abuse and corruption are often at greatest risk, particularly in states where criminal groups compete for territory and influence.

Northern Mexico has seen sustained violence tied to drug trafficking, migrant smuggling, fuel theft, extortion and other illicit economies. In many communities, journalists say criminal organizations attempt to dictate what can be reported — and what must remain invisible.

The result is a spreading climate of self-censorship. Some local newspapers no longer publish bylines on crime stories. Radio hosts avoid mentioning cartel names. Independent reporters remove articles from websites after threats. Others abandon journalism altogether.

“You learn there are words you cannot say,” said “María,” a journalist from another northern Mexican state who is seeking asylum in the US after receiving threats related to her reporting on missing persons. “You learn that silence can be a survival strategy. But silence also means the public loses the truth.”

María said she fled after men she did not recognize appeared outside her home and later followed her teenage son. She crossed into Texas with documents she hopes will support her asylum claim, including copies of her published work and threatening messages.

“I felt guilty leaving,” she said. “But what kind of mother would I be if I waited for them to kill me?”

## Seeking asylum in the United States

Under US law, asylum seekers must show they have a well-founded fear of persecution based on protected grounds such as political opinion or membership in a particular social group. Journalists fleeing threats may argue that their reporting placed them at risk because of political opinion or because they belong to a targeted group of media workers.

But winning asylum can be difficult. Applicants must navigate a complex immigration system, often without attorneys, while proving that the danger they face is specific, serious and that their government is unable or unwilling to protect them.

In El Paso, immigration attorneys and aid groups say they have seen journalists arrive with evidence of threats, published investigations, police reports and letters from editors. Some enter at ports of entry; others request protection after crossing the border. Many spend months or years waiting for hearings.

“The burden is high,” said an immigration attorney in Texas who has represented Mexican asylum seekers, including journalists. “You have to document not only that you were threatened, but why you were threatened and why the state could not protect you. That is especially hard for people who fled quickly.”

For journalists, the process can be emotionally punishing. Some say they are afraid to speak publicly because any attention could endanger family members in Mexico. Others continue reporting from exile under pseudonyms, while some work outside journalism to support themselves as their cases move forward.

Luis said he wants to keep writing but worries that publishing again could renew the threats.

“I crossed the border, but the fear crossed with me,” he said.

## Families left behind

For many fleeing journalists, the most painful part is leaving family members behind.

Luis’s wife and children remain in Mexico while he tries to find legal help and a stable place to live in El Paso. He speaks with them by encrypted messaging apps and avoids discussing details by phone. He said his children know only that he had to leave for “work problems.”

“I don’t know when I will see them again,” he said. “That is the punishment — not just the threats, but the separation.”

María said she brought one child with her but left elderly parents behind. She worries that the people who threatened her may target relatives to pressure her to return or stay silent.

Press freedom groups say such fears are not unfounded. Threats against journalists often extend to spouses, children and parents, creating a powerful incentive to stop reporting even after leaving the country.

“The violence is not only physical,” the advocate said. “It is psychological, economic and familial. It is designed to erase the journalist from public life.”

## Impunity fuels exile

Mexican officials have repeatedly said they are committed to protecting journalists and investigating attacks against the press. But advocates say prosecutions remain rare compared with the scale of the violence.

When cases go unsolved, they say, criminal groups and corrupt officials learn that threats can force reporters into silence with little consequence.

“Exile is becoming part of the playbook,” said a media rights researcher who monitors attacks in Mexico. “If you can scare a journalist into leaving, you don’t need to kill them. The community still loses its watchdog.”

In some towns, the departure of one reporter can leave entire regions without independent local coverage. Stories about disappearances, corruption, environmental damage or police abuse may never be reported. Residents then rely on rumor, official statements or social media posts that can be manipulated by criminal groups.

María said that is what haunts her most.

“They did not only threaten me,” she said. “They threatened the people’s right to know.”

## Waiting in El Paso

El Paso has long been a crossing point for people fleeing violence in Mexico and Central America. For Mexican journalists, the city can feel both safe and uncomfortably close to home. From parts of El Paso, Ciudad Juárez is visible across the Rio Grande — a reminder that danger may be only minutes away, even as the US asylum process stretches into uncertainty.

At shelters and legal clinics, journalists blend in with other asylum seekers: families fleeing extortion, migrants escaping gang threats, people hoping US law will recognize the danger they left behind.

Luis spends his days gathering documents for his case. He has printed articles bearing his name, saved screenshots of threats and written a timeline of the events that pushed him to flee. He is also trying to obtain letters from colleagues, though he worries asking for help could put them at risk.

At night, he checks Mexican news sites from his phone. Sometimes he sees stories he would have covered himself. Sometimes he sees nothing at all from the places where he knows violence is continuing.

“That silence tells me everything,” he said.

For now, his future depends on a legal system he is still trying to understand. He hopes an asylum officer or immigration judge will believe that journalism made him a target — and that returning to Mexico could cost him his life.

“I am not asking the United States to make me rich,” Luis said. “I am asking for the chance to survive and, one day, to write freely again.”

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a human-interest news story about people escaping violence and corruption in Mexico, especially reporters and police chiefs, and how their asylum cases illustrate the dangers posed by drug cartels.
counterfactuals.output:
**Fleeing the Cartels: Mexican Reporters and Police Chiefs Seek Safety Across the Border**

When the threats first arrived, the journalist tried to treat them like background noise — another grim part of reporting in a region where drug cartels have long operated with impunity.

Then came the calls to her family.

“They knew where my children went to school,” she said, sitting in a small apartment in the United States, where she is seeking asylum. “They told me I could keep writing, but I should start buying flowers for my own funeral.”

Her story is echoed by a growing number of Mexicans who say they fled not only cartel violence, but also corruption so deep that the usual places people turn for protection — police stations, city halls, prosecutors’ offices — could not be trusted. Among them are reporters who investigated organized crime and public officials, and police chiefs who say they were ordered to cooperate with criminal groups or die.

Their asylum claims offer a window into the dangers facing those who challenge cartel power in Mexico, where criminal organizations have expanded far beyond drug trafficking into extortion, kidnapping, fuel theft, migrant smuggling and control of local politics. For people who cross them, the consequences can be immediate and brutal.

The journalist, who asked that her name not be published because relatives remain in Mexico, said she had spent years covering municipal corruption, disappearances and cartel activity in her home state. She was accustomed to warnings from public officials who disliked her stories. But after she reported on alleged links between police officers and a criminal group, the threats changed.

A man approached her outside her newsroom and told her to stop “digging.” Soon after, she said, a source warned that her name had appeared on a list circulated by gunmen. She reported the threats to authorities, but nothing happened.

“It felt like filing a complaint with the same people who wanted me quiet,” she said.

Mexico is one of the most dangerous countries in the world for journalists, according to press freedom organizations, which have documented killings, disappearances and intimidation of reporters, particularly those covering local crime and corruption. While high-profile national reporters may have visibility that offers some protection, local journalists often work with little institutional support in communities where officials, police and criminals may be closely intertwined.

For former police commanders, the danger can be just as severe.

One ex-police chief from a small town in northern Mexico said his trouble began shortly after he took the job. Within weeks, he said, armed men demanded that his officers ignore cartel vehicles moving through the area. Later, they told him he was expected to provide patrol schedules and identify officers who could be bribed.

When he refused, he said, gunmen left a message outside his home.

“They didn’t ask again,” he said. “They said I had already chosen sides.”

He fled with his wife and children after an ambush killed two officers under his command. He believes the attack was meant for him.

In asylum proceedings, applicants must show more than generalized fear of violence. They must demonstrate that they were targeted for specific reasons recognized under asylum law, and that their government was unable or unwilling to protect them. For Mexicans fleeing cartel violence, that can be difficult. U.S. immigration courts often examine whether the harm was criminal rather than political, whether police protection was truly unavailable, and whether the person could safely relocate within Mexico.

But attorneys and advocates say cases involving journalists and law enforcement officials can reveal patterns that go beyond ordinary crime. Reporters may be targeted for exposing corruption or cartel abuses. Police chiefs may be threatened because they resist cartel control or refuse to participate in criminal networks. In both cases, the danger can follow them across state lines, especially when powerful organizations have national reach or official protection.

“The cartels don’t operate in a vacuum,” said one immigration attorney who has represented Mexican asylum seekers. “The strongest cases often involve evidence that criminal groups had help — or at least tolerance — from local authorities.”

That evidence can include police reports that led nowhere, threatening messages, news articles, human rights reports, and testimony about attacks on colleagues. But gathering documents can be risky. Some applicants leave quickly, carrying little more than identification papers and whatever proof they saved on their phones.

The human cost of waiting is heavy. Asylum cases can take years. During that time, families live in uncertainty, often separated from relatives still in danger. Some struggle to find work authorization, housing and counseling. Children adapt to new schools while parents check the news from home, scanning for names they recognize.

The former police chief said he still feels guilty for leaving.

“I wore a badge,” he said. “I told people to trust the law. Then I learned the law could not protect even me.”

The journalist keeps a notebook in her living room, though she no longer writes under her byline. She misses the rhythm of the newsroom — the phone calls, the deadlines, the sense that telling the truth mattered. But she also remembers the funerals of colleagues, and the silence that followed.

“I did not leave because I wanted a better job,” she said. “I left because they were going to kill me.”

For asylum seekers like her, the courtroom question is whether that fear fits within the boundaries of U.S. law. But their stories point to a broader crisis: in parts of Mexico, the people tasked with exposing or confronting criminal power can become its most vulnerable targets.

And for those who escape, safety is not the same as peace.

“I am alive,” the journalist said. “But I am still waiting to know if I am allowed to stay alive here.”
